Let \(G=(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)_{i,j}\) be the Gram matrix of the basis. Then \(G\) is positive definite, \(G_{ii}=1\), and the Gram matrix of the dual basis is \(G^{-1}\). Hence
\[
(G^{-1})_{ii}=\|w_i\|^2=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{tr}G=4,\qquad \operatorname{tr}G^{-1}=8.
\]

Set
\[
a=\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\qquad b=\frac{\eta}{2}.
\]
Since \(\varepsilon_i,\eta_i\in\{-1,1\}\) and \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\eta_i=0\), the vectors \(a,b\) are orthonormal in \(\mathbb R^4\). Also
\[
\left\|\sum_i\varepsilon_i v_i\right\|^2=\varepsilon^TG\varepsilon=4a^TGa,
\]
and similarly for \(\eta\). So the desired product is
\[
4\sqrt{(a^TGa)(b^TGb)}.
\]

Let the eigenvalues of \(G\) be
\[
\lambda_1\ge \lambda_2\ge \lambda_3\ge \lambda_4>0.
\]
By Ky Fan’s inequality,
\[
a^TGa+b^TGb\le \lambda_1+\lambda_2.
\]
Let \(u=\lambda_1+\lambda_2\). Since \(\sum\lambda_i=4\), we have \(\lambda_3+\lambda_4=4-u\). Also
\[
8=\sum_{i=1}^4\frac1{\lambda_i}
\ge \frac{4}{u}+\frac{4}{4-u},
\]
using \(\frac1x+\frac1y\ge \frac4{x+y}\) twice. Thus
\[
8\ge \frac{16}{u(4-u)},
\]
so
\[
u(4-u)\ge 2.
\]
This gives
\[
u\le 2+\sqrt2.
\]
Therefore
\[
(a^TGa)(b^TGb)\le \left(\frac{a^TGa+b^TGb}{2}\right)^2
\le \left(1+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2.
\]
Hence the product is at most
\[
4\left(1+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)=4+2\sqrt2.
\]

It remains to show this is attainable. Let
\[
t=1+\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad s=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},
\]
and define
\[
G=t(aa^T+bb^T)+s(I-aa^T-bb^T).
\]
Because \(a_i^2=b_i^2=\frac14\), each diagonal entry of \(G\) is
\[
\frac t2+\frac s2=1.
\]
Also
\[
G^{-1}=\frac1t(aa^T+bb^T)+\frac1s(I-aa^T-bb^T),
\]
and each diagonal entry is
\[
\frac12\left(\frac1t+\frac1s\right)=2,
\]
since \(ts=\frac12\) and \(t+s=2\). Thus this \(G\) is a valid Gram matrix, and \(a,b\) are eigenvectors with eigenvalue \(t\). Therefore the product equals
\[
4t=4+2\sqrt2.
\]

\[
\boxed{4+2\sqrt2}
\]
